nameStory: The Tundra Swan gets its name from its preferred breeding grounds in the Arctic tundra, where these elegant birds nest during the brief northern summer. In North America, they're also called Whistling Swans because of their musical calls that sound like gentle flute notes floating across the water. The scientific name 'columbianus' comes from the Columbia River, where early naturalists first formally described this species.
description: Tundra Swans are graceful white waterfowl that are smaller than their more common Mute Swan cousins. These Arctic travelers have pure white plumage, long curved necks, and black bills that often show a small yellow spot near the eye. Adults typically weigh 10-18 pounds with wingspans reaching 5-6 feet. They're long-distance migrants that pass through New England during spring and fall, creating magical moments for wildlife watchers.

idTips.label: Bill pattern
idTips.description: Look for a completely black bill with often a small yellow teardrop-shaped spot near the eye - this yellow marking feels smooth and looks like paint dabbed on, unlike the orange knob of Mute Swans

idTips.label: Neck posture
idTips.description: Holds neck straight up like a periscope when alert, rather than the curved S-shape of Mute Swans - gives them a more formal, upright appearance

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Produces clear, musical honking calls that sound like distant trumpets or flutes - much more vocal than the generally silent Mute Swan

idTips.label: Head shape
idTips.description: Has a more angular, wedge-shaped head profile compared to the rounded head of Mute Swans - the forehead slopes straight back from the bill

idTips.label: Size comparison
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than Mute Swans when seen together - about the size of a large goose rather than the massive bulk of Mute Swans

habitat: In New England, Tundra Swans are spotted on large bodies of open water during migration, including coastal bays, large lakes, reservoirs, and flooded agricultural fields. They prefer shallow areas where they can tip forward to reach underwater vegetation with their long necks. Look for them in places like Plum Island, the Connecticut River valley, and large inland lakes during peak migration times.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs from mid-March through April, when flocks pass through heading to Arctic breeding grounds. Listen for their musical calls overhead and scan large bodies of water for white forms.
seasonality.summer: Extremely rare in New England during summer as they're on Arctic breeding grounds. Any summer sightings would likely be injured birds or stragglers.
seasonality.fall: Return migration happens from October through December, often in family groups. Young birds may show grayish tingeing on head and neck feathers.
seasonality.winter: Uncommon winter visitors, mainly along the coast where waters remain unfrozen. Most continue south to the Chesapeake Bay and Carolina coasts.

funFact: Tundra Swans can live over 20 years and are so faithful to their mates that if one dies, the survivor may never breed again - they literally mate for life in the truest sense, sometimes remaining single for years after losing their partner.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Mute Swans, but remember 'Yellow spot, Tundra's got it' - Tundra Swans have the yellow marking on their black bills while Mute Swans have orange bills with a black knob. Tundra Swans are also much more vocal and hold their necks straighter.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Tundra' Swans, many birders still know them by their old name 'Whistling Swans,' which was changed in 1983 when scientists lumped the North American and European populations together. Don't be confused if you hear older birders or guides using the whistling swan name - they're talking about the same bird.
compareHints: Tundra Swans are much smaller than Trumpeter Swans and have yellow spots on their bills, while Trumpeters have all-black bills and deeper, more bugle-like calls. Compared to the common Mute Swan, Tundras are smaller, more vocal, hold their necks straighter, and have black bills with yellow spots instead of orange bills with black knobs. Mute Swans also often hold their wings slightly raised in an aggressive arch, which Tundra Swans rarely do.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike Trumpeter Swans, which have straight black bills and are much larger, Mute Swans have that telltale orange bill with black markings.
Trumpeter Swans are larger and more vocal than Mute Swans, with completely black bills versus the Mute Swan's orange bill with black knob.

Unlike the common Mute Swan with its white plumage and orange bill, or the Trumpeter and Tundra Swans with their white bodies and black bills, the Black Swan is the only swan species with entirely black plumage.
Compared to the much more common mute swan, whooper swans lack the orange bill and prominent forehead knob, instead showing that diagnostic yellow-and-black bill pattern.
Unlike our familiar Mute Swan with its all-white plumage and orange bill, the Black-necked Swan's dramatic two-toned coloring is unmistakable.
